    75 White Clematis

    Names

    Common name – White Clematis

    Scientific name – Clematis ligusticifolia

    Other names – k’ets’usnínina

    Fig 75.1: Close-up of Western White Clematis flowers, highlighting their four petal-like sepals.

    Fig 75.2: A Western White Clematis vine covered in fluffy, feathery seed heads in its natural habitat.

    General Information

    White Clematis, primarily referring to species like Clematis ligusticifolia (Western White Clematis) and Clematis virginiana (Virgin’s Bower), holds significant medicinal importance in Indigenous North American traditional medicine systems [8], [10] . These climbing vines, members of the Ranunculaceae family, contain potent bioactive compounds that have been carefully utilized by Native American tribes for centuries [2], [8] . Known for their vesicant (blister-causing) properties when used improperly [1], [4] , these plants require extensive traditional knowledge for safe preparation and application [2] . Indigenous healers have developed sophisticated methods to harness their therapeutic benefits while minimizing toxicity, using them primarily for neurological conditions, skin ailments, and pain management [8], [10] .

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    The plant was sometimes prepared in very dilute decoctions from its leaves and stems to ease migraine headaches or other sharp pains of the head [2], [10] . Even a few drops could calm the throbbing behind the eyes or release pressure in the temples, but the preparation had to be precise [2] . Too much could make one ill [10] .

    Carefully prepared tinctures were used to steady the spirit in times of anxiety or restlessness, and infusions made from the stems, sometimes mixed with other plants like milkweed, were taken for backaches or deep muscle pain [8] . The plant was also used to treat gout and rheumatism, either as a light tea or through topical applications that soothed swollen joints [10] . In ceremonies, its stems were burned or infused for ritual use, believed to help open the mind and body to spiritual insight [2], [8] . The plant’s extracts, when properly prepared and controlled, were said to bring visions and guide those seeking wisdom during vision quests [2] .

    Fresh leaves were crushed into poultices to clean cuts, infections, and wounds, their antiseptic qualities helping the skin recover [8], [10] . The juice of the fresh plant, though caustic, was applied carefully to remove warts or bring out inflammation in localized areas [10] .

    Biochemical Basis for Medicinal Properties

    Primary Bioactive Compounds

    1. Protoanemonin (Primary Active Compound) [9]

    • Chemical Formula: C₅H₄O₂
    • Structure: Unsaturated γ-lactone
    • Properties: Highly vesicant, antimicrobial, analgesic in small doses [1], [4], [9]
    • Mechanism: Cell membrane disruption, enzyme inhibition
    • Distribution: Higher concentrations in leaves and stems [4]

    2. Anemonin (Dimerization Product) [5], [9]

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₀H₈O₄
    • Formation: Protoanemonin dimer formed during processing
    • Properties: Less toxic than protoanemonin, anti-inflammatory [5], [9]
    • Stability: More stable compound formed during drying

    3. Triterpene Saponins [3], [7]

    Major Types:

    • Oleanolic acid derivatives
    • Hederagenin-based saponins
    • Ursolic acid derivatives

    Properties:

    • Hemolytic activity [3]
    • Anti-inflammatory effects [3]
    • Cytotoxic properties
    • Immunomodulatory activity

    4. Flavonoids [6]

    • Quercetin derivatives
    • Kaempferol glycosides
    • Rutin compounds
    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, vascular protective

    5. Additional Bioactive Compounds [6]

    • Alkaloids: Various nitrogen-containing compounds
    • Lignans: Phenolic compounds with estrogenic activity
    • Coumarins: Anticoagulant and antimicrobial properties
    • Volatile oils: Contributing to antimicrobial effects

    Chemical Structure of a Key Compound

    Protoanemonin

    Fig 75.3: Chemical structure of protoanemonin, the primary bioactive and vesicant compound found in White Clematis.

    Mechanism of Action

    Vesicant Activity [1]

    • Protoanemonin action: Direct cellular damage through protein denaturation
    • Inflammatory response: Localized immune activation
    • Traditional use: Controlled inflammation for therapeutic purposes

    Analgesic Properties [5], [9]

    • Neuronal membrane stabilization by low-dose protoanemonin
    • Inflammation reduction through saponin activity
    • Endorphin release triggered by mild irritation

    Antimicrobial Activity [6], [9]

    • Cell wall disruption by protoanemonin
    • Protein denaturation in microbial cells
    • Oxidative stress induction in pathogens

    Anti-inflammatory Mechanisms [3], [6]

    • Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition by flavonoids and saponins
    • Cytokine modulation through triterpene compounds
    • Immune system regulation by saponin fractions

    Pharmacological Activities

    Activity Responsible Compounds Mechanism Traditional Application
    Analgesic Protoanemonin (low doses), saponins Neuronal stabilization, inflammation reduction Headaches, backache, joint pain
    Antimicrobial Protoanemonin, volatile oils Cell membrane disruption Skin infections, wound care
    Anti-inflammatory Flavonoids, triterpene saponins COX inhibition, cytokine modulation Rheumatism, gout, joint conditions
    Vesicant Protoanemonin Direct cellular damage Controlled therapeutic inflammation
    Nervine Alkaloids, low-dose protoanemonin Neurological modulation Nervous disorders, anxiety

    Biochemical Reactions

    Protoanemonin Formation [9]

    Ranunculin (glycoside) → [Enzymatic hydrolysis] → Protoanemonin + Glucose

    Protoanemonin to Anemonin Conversion [9]

    2 Protoanemonin → [Dimerization] → Anemonin

    This reaction occurs naturally during plant processing and storage

    Protein Interaction [9]

    Protoanemonin + Protein -SH groups → Protein-S-Protoanemonin adducts

    Safety and Toxicological Considerations

    Toxicity Profile

    • Acute toxicity: Severe skin and mucous membrane irritation [1]
    • Systemic effects: Gastrointestinal distress, renal damage
    • Lethal dose: Variable, but small amounts can cause severe reactions

    Traditional Safety Measures

    • Extreme dilution: Use of minute quantities
    • Specific preparation methods: Traditional processing to reduce toxicity
    • Experienced practitioners: Knowledge passed through generations
    • External vs. internal use: Careful distinction in applications

    Modern Research Validation

    Confirmed Activities

    • Antimicrobial properties: Validated against various pathogens [6], [9]
    • Anti-inflammatory effects: Demonstrated in laboratory studies [3], [5]
    • Analgesic activity: Confirmed in controlled studies
    • Cytotoxic properties: Active against certain cancer cell lines

    Safety Studies

    • Toxicity assessments: Confirmed traditional safety concerns
    • Dosage guidelines: Support for traditional dilution practices
    • Preparation methods: Validation of traditional processing techniques

    Important Disclaimers

    Critical Safety Warning : White Clematis species are highly toxic and can cause severe skin burns, systemic poisoning, and death if improperly prepared or used. This information is provided for educational purposes only.

    Cultural Respect : Traditional Indigenous knowledge represents thousands of years of accumulated wisdom and should be approached with respect. Proper cultural protocols and permissions should be observed when accessing or using traditional knowledge.

    Medical Disclaimer : Never attempt to prepare or use Clematis species medicinally without extensive training and guidance from qualified practitioners. Modern medical supervision is essential for any therapeutic applications.

    76 Whitebark Pine

    Names

    Common name – Whitebark Pine

    Scientific name – Pinus albicaulis

    Other names – zaxalmíxważ’

    Important Note : Whitebark Pine is considered a species of conservation concern, so any traditional or modern use must be approached with appropriate conservation considerations and respect for Indigenous knowledge systems. [16]

    Fig 76.1: A close-up photograph of a Whitebark Pine cone and needles covered in resin droplets.

    Fig 76.2: A small, stunted Whitebark Pine tree growing on a rocky alpine ridge against a blue sky.

    General Information

    Whitebark Pine ( Pinus albicaulis ) is a high-elevation conifer native to the mountainous regions of western North America, including the Rocky Mountains, Sierra Nevada, and Cascade Range. [6] This hardy tree, which often marks the treeline in subalpine environments, has been an important resource for Indigenous peoples of the region for centuries. [5],[9] Like other pine species, Whitebark Pine contains valuable medicinal compounds in its bark, needles, and resin. [4],[9] Indigenous communities, particularly those in the interior Pacific Northwest, Northern Rockies, and Great Basin regions, have traditionally utilized various parts of this tree for medicinal purposes, though its high-elevation habitat has made it less accessible than lower-elevation pine species. [5],[9] The tree’s medicinal properties are primarily attributed to its rich content of monoterpenes, diterpenes, and phenolic compounds found in its resin and bark. [4]

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    The needles and inner bark were boiled into teas or used in steam baths to treat coughs, colds, and lung troubles like bronchitis and pneumonia. [5],[9] The same teas were also taken for stomach pain or digestive troubles, helping the body to settle and heal from within. [5],[9]

    The resin or pitch of the Whitebark Pine was considered medicine for the skin. It was softened by the fire and placed directly on wounds, burns, or infections to draw out impurities and seal the skin. [5],[9] Sometimes it was mixed into salves or poultices with bark, creating an antiseptic that prevented infection and encouraged healing. [5],[9] For aching joints and sore muscles, baths made from the bark or needles brought relief, their warmth soothing pain from rheumatism or long days of work. [5],[9] Those who suffered from kidney or urinary troubles also drank mild teas made from the inner bark, which were said to cleanse and strengthen the body’s waters. [9]

    The seeds, known as pine nuts, were gathered from the cones and eaten raw or roasted, offering energy and strength during the colder months. [9] The fresh needles were also chewed or brewed to ward off scurvy. [9] In ceremonies, its branches and needles were burned, the smoke cleansing both body and spirit. [5],[9]

    Biochemical Basis for Medicinal Properties

    Primary Bioactive Compounds

    1. Monoterpenes (Essential Oil Components)

    α-Pinene (Primary Active Compound)

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₀H₁₆
    • Concentration: 25-90% of essential oil in pine species [4],[8]
    • Structure: Bicyclic monoterpene
    • Properties: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, bronchodilator, memory enhancer [8],[10],[11]

    β-Pinene

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₀H₁₆
    • Concentration: 5-25% of essential oil [4],[8]
    • Structure: Bicyclic monoterpene (isomer of α-pinene)
    • Properties: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, analgesic [8],[10],[11]

    Limonene

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₀H₁₆
    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial [13]

    Myrcene

    • Properties: Analgesic, anti-inflammatory, muscle relaxant [15]

    2. Diterpenes and Resin Acids

    Abietic Acid

    • Chemical Formula: C₂₀H₃₀O₂
    • Source: Rosin fraction of pine resin
    • Properties: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory [12]

    Pimaric Acid

    • Chemical Formula : C₂₀H₃₀O₂
    • Properties : Antimicrobial, wound healing [12]

    Dehydroabietic Acid

    Antimicrobial Activity

    Anti-inflammatory Properties

    • Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition by monoterpenes and phenolics [7],[11]
    • Lipoxygenase inhibition reducing inflammatory mediators [14]
    • Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway modulation [14]
    • Cytokine production reduction [11],[14]

    Respiratory Benefits

    • Bronchodilation through β-adrenergic receptor activation [11]
    • Mucolytic activity facilitating mucus clearance [8]
    • Antimicrobial action against respiratory pathogens [8],[11]
    • Anti-inflammatory effects in airways [11]

    Antioxidant Mechanisms

    • Free radical scavenging by phenolic compounds [7],[14]
    • Metal chelation by flavonoids [1]
    • Enzyme system support (glutathione, catalase) [1],[14]
    • Lipid peroxidation inhibition [7],[14]

    Monoterpene Biosynthesis

    Safety and Dosage Considerations

    Safety Profile

    • Generally safe when used traditionally in appropriate doses [5]
    • Skin sensitization possible with concentrated resin [12]
    • Gastrointestinal irritation with excessive internal use [4]
    • Respiratory irritation with excessive inhalation [8]

    Traditional Dosage Guidelines

    • Needle tea: 1-2 teaspoons dried needles per cup of hot water
    • Bark decoction: Small amounts of inner bark, well-diluted
    • Topical resin: Applied sparingly to affected areas
    • Steam inhalation: Brief exposure to needle-infused steam

    Modern Research Validation

    Confirmed Activities

    • Antimicrobial properties: Validated against various pathogens including bacteria and fungi [11],[12]
    • Anti-inflammatory effects: Demonstrated in multiple laboratory and clinical studies [11],[14]
    • Antioxidant activity: Confirmed through various assay methods [1],[14]
    • Respiratory benefits: Supported by pharmacological research on monoterpenes [8],[11]

    Clinical Applications

    • Respiratory health: Modern pine needle extracts used in cough preparations
    • Topical treatments: Pine-derived compounds in wound care products
    • Aromatherapy: Essential oils for respiratory and mood benefits
    • Nutritional supplements: Pine bark extracts for antioxidant support

    Important Disclaimers

    Cultural Respect : This information represents traditional knowledge systems that should be approached with appropriate respect and cultural protocols. Traditional Indigenous knowledge is the intellectual property of Indigenous communities.

    Medical Disclaimer : This information is provided for educational purposes only. Traditional preparations should not be attempted without proper guidance from qualified practitioners familiar with both traditional methods and modern safety considerations.

    Conservation Note : Whitebark Pine is considered a species of conservation concern in many areas due to climate change, disease, and other threats. Sustainable harvesting practices should always be followed, and in many areas, the species may be protected by law. [16]

    Identification Warning : Proper botanical identification is essential, as some plants may be confused with toxic species. Always ensure correct identification before any medicinal use.

    77 Wild Asparagus

    Names

    Common Name – Wild Asparagus

    Scientific Name : Asparagus officinalis

    Other Names: Sparrowgrass, garden asparagus

    Fig 77.1: Mature wild asparagus plant growing along a trail near Kamloops, British Columbia, showing its characteristic feathery foliage.

    Image Source: https://kamloopstrails.net/news/wild-asparagus/

    The young shoots of wild asparagus are an important food source. While low in calories, asparagus contains many vitamins and minerals and is high in protein and dietary fiber which is important for digestive health and may help reduce the risk of diabetes. [2] Wild asparagus also contains saponins, flavonoids and sterols. [1]

    Fig 77.2: Fresh, edible young wild asparagus shoots emerging from the ground in the Similkameen region.

    Image Source: https://infotel.ca/inwine/okanagan-asparagus-season-is-underway/it82118

    The dietary fibre in asparagus contains high quantities of pectin (structure shown below), as well as cellulose and lignin. [4] It is also interesting to note that, although the young shoots are eaten because the taste and texture becomes less palatable as the stalks age, the young shoots actually contain more nutrients than the older shoots do as well. [1]

    Fig 77.3: Chemical structure of pectin, a major structural heteropolysaccharide found in the dietary fiber of wild asparagus.

    Although edible, handling wild asparagus can cause dermatitis and so should be collected and handled with care. It is also possible to have an allergy to asparagus which may result in asthma- like symptoms. [3]

    78 Wild Strawberry

    Names

    Common name – Wild Strawberry

    Scientific name – Fragaria virginiana

    Other names – skw’eláp

    Fig 78.1: A cluster of Wild Strawberry (Fragaria virginiana) leaves with two ripe red berries and one unripe berry.

    Fig 78.2: Close-up of Wild Strawberry (Fragaria virginiana) leaves and multiple delicate white flowers.

    General Information

    Wild Strawberry, primarily Fragaria virginiana (Wild Strawberry) and Fragaria vesca (Woodland Strawberry), holds profound cultural and medicinal significance for Indigenous peoples across North America. [1], [5], [7] These small, perennial plants of the Rose family (Rosaceae) are revered not only for their nutritious fruits but also for the therapeutic properties of their leaves, roots, and runners. In many Indigenous traditions, the strawberry is considered sacred – the “leader of all plants” and often associated with the heart, love, and the life force itself. The entire plant contains a rich array of bioactive compounds including ellagitannins, flavonoids, phenolic acids, and vitamin C, which contribute to its wide-ranging medicinal applications. [3] Traditional Indigenous knowledge systems have recognized wild strawberry as a gentle yet effective remedy for numerous ailments, particularly those affecting the digestive system, skin, and urogenital tract. [1], [5], [7]

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    Its leaves were steeped into gentle teas that supported the body’s water flow, cleansing the kidneys and bladder and helping those who suffered from urinary troubles or water retention. These same teas were used for heart and circulation health, believed to strengthen the spirit and calm the emotions. For women, the leaves were taken as a mild infusion and they brought balance to the body, easing menstrual irregularities and supporting the womb during pregnancy. [1], [5], [7]

    The roots, when prepared as astringent teas, were used to calm diarrhea and settle the stomach, while the leaves, chewed fresh or dried into poultices, were pressed onto burns, sores, or cuts to cool inflammation and draw out infection. They were also used as washes for the eyes, to soothe redness and irritation caused by smoke or illness. When mixed with animal fat, the leaves and runners formed salves that treated rashes, eczema, and skin infections, restoring the skin’s strength and softness. During fever or weakness, a cold infusion of the entire plant was given to bring the body back to balance and renew its energy. [1], [5], [7]

    Biochemical Basis for Medicinal Properties

    Primary Bioactive Compounds

    1. Ellagitannins (Hydrolyzable Tannins) [8]

    Major Ellagitannins in Fragaria :

    • Agrimoniin – Primary ellagitannin
    • Potentillin – Secondary ellagitannin
    • Sanguiin H-6 – Complex ellagitannin
    • Lambertianin C – Large molecular weight ellagitannin

    Properties :

    • Strong astringent activity
    • Antimicrobial effects
    • Anti-inflammatory properties
    • Antioxidant capacity
    • Wound healing promotion

    2. Ellagic Acid and Derivatives [3], [8]

    Ellagic Acid

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₄H₆O₈
    • Source: Released from ellagitannin hydrolysis
    • Concentration: Variable in leaves and fruits
    • Properties: Potent antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial

    • Enhanced bioavailability

    • Extended biological activity

    • Properties: Anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, cardiovascular protective

    • Kaempferol-3-glucoside
    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, diuretic

    Catechins and Proanthocyanidins

    • (-)-Epicatechin
    • Procyanidin dimers and oligomers
    • Properties: Vascular protective, astringent, antimicrobial

    • Immune system support
    • Collagen synthesis

    Astringent Properties [8]

    • Protein precipitation by tannins and ellagitannins

    • Wound healing through tissue tightening and protection

    Activity Responsible Compounds Mechanism Traditional Application

    Anti-inflammatory Quercetin, ellagic acid, catechins COX/LOX inhibition, cytokine modulation Skin inflammation, digestive irritation
    Antioxidant Ellagic acid, flavonoids, vitamin C Free radical scavenging, metal chelation General health, aging, wound healing

    Biochemical Reactions

    Ellagitannin Hydrolysis

    Ellagitannin + H₂O → [Enzymatic/Acid hydrolysis] → Ellagic acid + Glucose + Gallic acid

    Antioxidant Reaction (Ellagic Acid)

    Ellagic acid + Free Radical → Ellagic acid radical + Neutralized radical ↓  Stable quinone form

    Tannin-Protein Binding

    Tannin + Protein → Tannin-Protein Complex (Precipitate)

    Flavonoid Metal Chelation

    Quercetin + Metal Ion (Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺) → Quercetin-Metal Complex

    Safety and Dosage Considerations

    Safety Profile

    • Generally safe when used in traditional preparations
    • Low toxicity compared to many medicinal plants
    • Possible allergic reactions in sensitive individuals
    • Mild gastrointestinal effects with excessive use

    Traditional Dosage Guidelines

    • Leaf tea: 1-2 teaspoons dried leaves per cup of hot water
    • Root decoction: Small amounts, well-diluted for astringent effects
    • Fresh applications: Direct application of chewed leaves for topical use
    • Maintenance doses: Regular, small amounts for ongoing health support

    Modern Research Validation

    Confirmed Activities [3], [4]

    • Antioxidant properties: Extensively validated through multiple assay methods
    • Anti-inflammatory effects: Confirmed in various laboratory and clinical studies
    • Antimicrobial activity: Demonstrated against bacteria, fungi, and viruses
    • Astringent properties: Validated for wound healing and digestive health
    • Cardiovascular benefits: Supported by research on flavonoids and proanthocyanidins

    Clinical Applications

    • Topical preparations: Commercial products for wound care and skin health
    • Dietary supplements: Standardized extracts for antioxidant support
    • Functional foods: Enhanced strawberry products for health benefits
    • Cosmetic applications: Anti-aging and skin protection formulations

    Bioavailability and Metabolism

    Absorption Patterns [2], [3]

    • Ellagic acid: Limited absorption, converted to urolithins by gut bacteria
    • Flavonoids: Variable absorption depending on glycoside forms
    • Tannins: Limited systemic absorption, primarily local effects
    • Vitamin C: Readily absorbed, water-soluble

    Metabolic Pathways [2], [3]

    Ellagitannins → [Gut bacteria] → Urolithins A, B, C, D Flavonoid glycosides → [Intestinal enzymes] → Aglycones + Sugars

    Cultural Respect : Wild strawberry holds sacred significance in many Indigenous traditions. This information should be approached with respect for Indigenous knowledge systems and cultural protocols.

    Medical Disclaimer : This information is provided for educational purposes only. Traditional preparations should not be attempted without proper guidance from qualified practitioners familiar with both traditional methods and modern safety considerations.

    Sustainable Harvesting : Always follow sustainable harvesting practices and respect local regulations. Wild strawberry populations should be preserved for future generations and ecosystem health.

    Identification Accuracy : Proper botanical identification is essential. While wild strawberries are generally safe, other plants may be confused with them. Always ensure correct identification before any medicinal use.

    Scientific name – Elaeagnus commutata

    Other names – Silverberry

    General Information

    Wolf Willow ( Elaeagnus commutata ), also known as Silverberry, is a hardy deciduous shrub native to western and boreal North America. [3, 8] This resilient plant, characterized by its distinctive silvery foliage and fragrant yellow flowers, has been a valuable resource for Indigenous peoples across the prairie provinces and northern regions for centuries. [1, 5] Indigenous peoples have traditionally utilized different parts of this plant for medicinal, ceremonial, and practical purposes. [1, 5] Wolf Willow’s medicinal properties stem from its rich content of bioactive compounds including flavonoids, phenolic acids, and other secondary metabolites that contribute to its anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, and healing properties. [2, 7] The plant’s ability to thrive in harsh prairie conditions and its multiple traditional applications have made it an important component of Indigenous pharmacopoeias across its natural range. [4, 5]

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    From the bark, teas were brewed to ease chest colds, coughs, and other breathing troubles, helping to clear the lungs and restore the voice. [1, 4] The same bark, when softened and mixed with animal grease, was rubbed onto frostbitten skin to draw out the cold and bring back warmth. [4, 5]

    The inner bark of Wolf Willow provided the strong fibers used to make ropes and baskets. [5] The seeds were turned into beads for regalia and spiritual objects, worn during dances and ceremonies. [5]

    Medicinally, the bark and leaves of Wolf Willow were also prepared into salves and poultices to treat wounds, cuts, and abrasions. [5] These same preparations were used to reduce swelling and ease joint pain, while mild teas from the inner bark soothed the stomach and supported digestion. [4, 5]

    • Chemical Formula: C₂₇H₃₀O₁₆
    • Properties: Vascular protective, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant

    • Anti-inflammatory effects: Inhibition of COX-1, COX-2 and corticosterone release confirmed as possible mechanism for therapeutic potential [2]

    • Multiple bioactivities: Numerous biological activities such as anti-inflammatory, antiedema, antinociceptive, and muscle relaxant functions [2]

    Clinical Relevance

    • Pain management: Widely used to relax muscles, kill pains, treat inflammation, ease fever and cure ulcers [2]

    80 Wolly Pussytoes

    Names

    Common name – Woolly Pussytoes

    Scientific name – Antennaria lanata

    Fig 80.1: Close-up of Woolly Pussytoes ( Antennaria lanata ) inflorescence.

    Fig 80.2: Woolly Pussytoes ( Antennaria lanata ) growing in its natural alpine habitat.

    General Information

    Woolly Pussytoes ( Antennaria lanata ) is a small, alpine perennial herb in the Asteraceae family, characterized by its distinctive woolly, silvery-white foliage that resembles cat’s paws. [3], [11] This hardy mountain plant is native to western North America, ranging from alpine and subalpine meadows across the northwestern United States and western Canada. [3], [11] Indigenous peoples of the Rocky Mountain and Pacific Northwest regions have traditionally utilized various Antennaria species, including Woolly Pussytoes, for their medicinal properties. [7] The plant’s dense, mat-forming growth habit and woolly texture have made it valuable not only for medicine but also for practical applications such as tinder and soft padding. [7] The medicinal properties of Antennaria species are attributed to their content of flavonoids, sesquiterpene lactones, and other bioactive compounds that contribute to their anti-inflammatory, respiratory, and digestive therapeutic effects. [1], [2]

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    When sickness touched the lungs, the leaves and flowers were brewed into a warm tea or used in steam inhalations to soothe coughs, loosen chest congestion, and bring relief to those struggling to breathe. The same gentle tea, when taken by mouth, calmed the stomach and helped with indigestion or mild gastritis, restoring comfort after illness or heavy meals. [5], [7] During the cold months, it was often given to those with fevers or colds to help the body recover. [5], [7]

    The woolly texture of the plant was used directly on the skin as a natural dressing for cuts, scrapes, and irritations. Its soft leaves acted as padding, protecting wounds from dirt while helping them to heal. [5], [7] For sore muscles and aching joints, the whole plant could be warmed and applied as a poultice to draw out pain and swelling. The plant’s gentle nature made it especially useful for sensitive skin and even for babies. The soft fibers were used as padding in cradles or as a natural lining for diapers. [5], [7]

    The flowers were burned in smudging rituals. [5]

    • Mechanism: Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) inhibition, enzyme modulation [4], [8]

    2. Flavonoids

    81 Yellow Mountain-Avens

    Names

    Common name – Yellow Mountain-Avens

    Scientific name – Dryas drummondii

    Fig 81.1: Yellow Mountain-Avens (Dryas drummondii) featuring its characteristic yellow flowers.

    Fig 81.2: Close-up view of Yellow Mountain-Avens showing intricate botanical structures.

    General Information:

    Yellow Mountain-Avens represents a group of alpine plants that include both Geum montanum (Alpine Avens) and Dryas drummondii (Yellow Mountain Avens), both belonging to the Rosaceae family. [4] These hardy perennial herbs thrive in mountainous and arctic regions across North America and Europe, adapting to harsh alpine conditions with their low-growing, mat-forming habit. [4,5] Indigenous peoples of mountainous regions have traditionally utilized these plants for various medicinal purposes, particularly for cardiovascular, urinary, and inflammatory conditions. [1,5] The plants’ distinctive yellow flowers and their ability to survive in extreme alpine environments have made them culturally significant as symbols of resilience and healing. [5] The medicinal properties of these species are attributed to their rich content of tannins, phenolic compounds, and essential oils, which contribute to their astringent, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial therapeutic effects. [2,3,6] Its root smells like clove. [3]

    Traditional Indigenous Uses

    Its roots and leaves could be made into a tea or decoction to help those suffering from heart weakness or poor circulation. [1] It was also used as a medicine for the kidneys and bladder, its cleansing properties helping to clear infections. [1]

    A mild infusion from the leaves or whole plant brought calm to the belly and restored appetite. [1] For coughs, chest congestion, and inflammation in the lungs, the leaves and flowers were boiled into teas or used as steam inhalations to clear the airways. [1] Its roots, when prepared as a stronger decoction, were taken to ease the aches of rheumatism and arthritis or applied to sore joints and muscles to reduce swelling. [1,5] Fresh plant material could be made into poultices or washes to help wounds heal more quickly and to treat skin irritations, rashes, or infections. [1,5]

    Yellow Mountain-Avens was respected as a general tonic. [1] It was said to “wake up the body” after long sickness and to bring a cooling peace to those burning with fever. [1]

    Biochemical Basis for Medicinal Properties

    Primary Bioactive Compounds (Based on Geum Genus Research) [2]

    1. Phenolic Compounds

    Eugenol (Primary Active Compound)

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₀H₁₂O₂
    • Source: Roots (clove-like aroma) [3]
    • Concentration: Variable, responsible for characteristic scent
    • Properties: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antiseptic
    • Traditional correlation: Wound healing, respiratory conditions [3]

    Gallic Acid

    • Chemical Formula: C₇H₆O₅
    • Properties: Strong antioxidant, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory
    • Mechanism: Free radical scavenging, enzyme inhibition
    • Traditional use: General healing, inflammatory conditions [2]

    Caffeic Acid

    • Chemical Formula: C₉H₈O₄
    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial
    • Traditional correlation: Skin conditions, wound healing [2]

    Chlorogenic Acid

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₆H₁₈O₉
    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, hepatoprotective
    • Traditional use: General wellness, digestive support [2]

    2. Tannins (High Concentration)

    Condensed Tannins (Proanthocyanidins)

    • Concentration: 10.5% in related Geum species
    • Properties: Astringent, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory
    • Mechanism: Protein binding, antimicrobial activity
    • Traditional use: Diarrhea, wound healing, skin conditions [2]

    Hydrolysable Tannins

    • Properties: Astringent, antimicrobial, antioxidant
    • Traditional correlation: Digestive disorders, external healing [2]

    3. Flavonoids

    Quercetin and Derivatives

    • Chemical Formula: C₁₅H₁₀O₇
    • Properties: Anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, vascular protective
    • Mechanism: COX inhibition, free radical scavenging
    • Traditional use: Cardiovascular support, inflammatory conditions [2,6]

    Kaempferol Glycosides

    • Properties: Antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective
    • Traditional correlation: Heart conditions, circulatory support [2]

    Rutin

    • Properties: Vascular strengthening, anti-inflammatory, antioxidant
    • Traditional use: Cardiovascular health, capillary fragility [2]

    4. Essential Oil Components

    Monoterpenes

    • α-Pinene: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, respiratory supportive
    • Limonene: Antioxidant, antimicrobial, digestive supportive
    • Linalool: Mild sedative, antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory

    Sesquiterpenes

    • β-Caryophyllene: Anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antimicrobial [3]
    • Germacrene-D: Antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory [3]

    Mechanism of Action

    Cardiovascular Support

    • Vasodilation by flavonoids and phenolic compounds
    • Antioxidant protection prevents cardiovascular damage
    • Anti-inflammatory effects in vascular tissues
    • Cardiotonic effects by specific glycosides [2]

    Anti-inflammatory Properties

    • Cyclooxygenase (COX) inhibition by flavonoids and eugenol
    • Lipoxygenase inhibition by phenolic compounds
    • Nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway modulation
    • Cytokine production reduction (TNF-α, IL-1β, IL-6) [2,6]

    Antimicrobial Activity

    • Protein binding by tannins

    Astringent and Wound Healing

    • Protein precipitation by tannins

    • Anti-inflammatory action in urinary tissues

    Relevant Biochemical Pathways

    Anti-inflammatory Pathway

    Eugenol/Flavonoids → COX-1/COX-2 inhibition → ↓ Prostaglandin synthesis → ↓ Inflammation [2,6]

    Antimicrobial Action

    Eugenol → Bacterial cell membrane → Membrane disruption → Cell lysis → Death [3]

    Tannin Astringent Effect

    Tannins + Proteins → Tannin-protein complexes → Tissue contraction → Hemostasis [2]

    Antioxidant Mechanism

    Flavonoids + ROS → Flavonoid radicals + H₂O (neutralized radicals) [2]

    Traditional Preparation Methods

    Cardiovascular Support Tea

    • Ingredients: Dried roots and leaves of Yellow Mountain-Avens
    • Method: Gentle decoction, simmered for 15-20 minutes
    • Dosage: Small amounts, 1-2 cups daily
    • Traditional use: Heart conditions, circulatory support [1,5]

    Kidney and Bladder Treatment

    • Preparation: Root tea preparation
    • Method: Hot water infusion of dried roots
    • Application: Internal consumption, 2-3 times daily
    • Benefits: Diuretic, anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial effects [1]

    Wound Healing Poultice

    • Method: Fresh plant material crushed and applied directly
    • Application: External application to wounds, cuts, abrasions
    • Active compounds: Tannins, eugenol, antimicrobial compounds
    • Benefits: Hemostatic, antimicrobial, healing acceleration [1,5]

    Anti-inflammatory Preparation

    • Ingredients: Whole plant material
    • Method: Traditional extraction methods
    • Application: Both internal and external use
    • Traditional correlation: Joint pain, muscle soreness, inflammatory conditions [1]

    Safety and Dosage Considerations

    Safety Profile

    • Generally safe when used traditionally in appropriate amounts
    • Mild gastrointestinal effects possible with high tannin content
    • No significant toxicity reported in traditional literature
    • Pregnancy considerations: Traditional caution advised [2]

    Traditional Dosage Guidelines

    • Internal use: 1-2 teaspoons of dried plant material per cup of water
    • External use: Applied as needed to affected areas
    • Frequency: 2-3 times daily for acute conditions
    • Duration: Short-term use for acute conditions, longer for chronic issues [1,2]

    Contraindications

    • High tannin sensitivity: May cause stomach irritation in sensitive individuals
    • Iron absorption: High tannin content may interfere with iron absorption
    • Pregnancy: Traditional caution during pregnancy and nursing
    • Medication interactions: Potential interactions with cardiovascular medications [2]

    Important Disclaimers

    Cultural Respect : Traditional Indigenous knowledge of Yellow Mountain-Avens represents centuries of accumulated wisdom and practical experience. This knowledge belongs to Indigenous communities and should be approached with appropriate respect, acknowledgment, and cultural protocols. [1,5]

    Limited Specific Research : While extensive research exists on related Geum species, specific studies on Dryas drummondii (Yellow Mountain-Avens) are limited. The medicinal properties described are based on traditional knowledge and research on closely related species. [2,4]

    Medical Disclaimer : This information is provided for educational purposes only. Traditional preparations should not be attempted without proper guidance from qualified practitioners familiar with both traditional methods and modern safety considerations. [2]

    Conservation Awareness : Yellow Mountain-Avens grows in sensitive alpine and arctic environments that may be vulnerable to climate change. Sustainable harvesting practices and conservation awareness are essential. [5]

    Proper Identification : Accurate botanical identification is crucial, especially in alpine environments where multiple similar species may occur. Consult with qualified botanists or traditional knowledge holders for proper plant identification. [4,5]
